text.body:
CLAUSE STRUCTURE IN THE PROSE DOCUMENTS OF QUMRAN CAVE 1 (1)
1. — My previous article on Qumrani clause structure (2) presents few or no facts which were previously unknown. Its novelty lies in the point of view from which these facts are regarded. The study of Hebrew clauses as composed, not of words, but of 'clause builders' permits very much easier description and comparison of clause structure. It is necessary, however, to justify the establishment of the clause builder class somewhat more fully than can be done merely by demonstrating its validity in the verbal clauses of one text. This study attempts to do this by analyzing all the clauses in the prose texts of Qumran Cave I in terms of clause-builders.
2. — The purpose of this study is, then, to analyze the structure of the clauses in the language used to write the theological texts of Qumran Cave I. In order to ensure that it is based on the simplest form of the language commonly in use, the study is restricted to prose texts (3). Quotations from the Old Testament in these texts, which are explicitly marked as quotations, are not, of course, included in this study. However, the Qumran texts are full of allusions to the Old Testament. These allusions are, for the purposes of this study, considered to be typical of the form of language used to write the theological texts of Qumran Cave I, and native to it. Such allusions are not, therefore, excluded from This study has received considerable benefit from the able criticism of an earlier draught by M. l'abbé J. CARMIGNAC. I would like here to express my thanks to him for his kind assistance. Revue de Qumrân, n° 12, t. 3, fasc. 4 (octobre 1962), p. 559-569. Henceforward referred to as "Order". The texts used are: 1 Q Serek, except the poetical sections at I, 24-II, 1; II, 2-4; II, 5-9, and columns X and XI; 1 Q Milḥamah except the poetical sections in XII, 7-16; XIX, 1-8; the non-biblical portions of 1 Q p Hab, 1 Q 14 and 1 Q 16; 1 Q 17; 1 Q 18; 1 Q 19; 1 Q 22; 1 Q 26; 1 Q Sa; 1 Q Sb (only the titles to the 'blessings'); 1 Q 29.
E. J. REVELL

3. — In order to clarify the point of view from which this study is written, a short account of the syntactical structure of the Hebrew language as here envisaged must be given. Most Hebrew grammars are written in terms of two levels of structure, ‘words’, and ‘clauses’. However a much more exact and detailed analysis can be carried out if further levels of structure are isolated for individual investigation. It is well known that words are formed of smaller units, known as morphemes (5). Morphemes are the basic units of syntactic structure. They combine to form the next larger unit, the word. The term ‘word’ is used here with the meaning ‘member of a grammatical word class’ (6). Word classes which can be most easily distinguished are: verb (v), noun (n) (7), pronoun, infinitive (i) (8), article (h), conjunction (c), and preposition (p). The remaining particles are more difficult to classify. The outline of a new scheme, with reasons for rejecting the old, is given below in § 7.
4. — Words are formed into ‘clause-builders’ (9). These are: V, the verbal element,—Ns, a nominal element showing concord with the bound pronoun in the verb form (10)—N, any other type of nominal element,—pN, a nominal element preceded by a preposition,—pI, an infinitive and its modifiers preceded by
Some justification for this viewpoint may be seen in the fact that the explicit quotations are all identical with, or very close to, the consonantal form of the received text of the Old Testament. The allusions, however, often appear to be quotations from the Old Testament which have been changed, in grammar and/or content, to fit the language and ideas of the author of the text. Compare, for example, 1 Q S II, 13 BRYT, YTBRK, YHY, with Deuteronomy 29, 18 'LH, WHTBRK, YHYH. In 1 Q S II, 14 the Qumrani ‘allusion’ becomes even farther removed from the Biblical original. Such changes would seem to stamp the Biblical original with the impress of Qumrani grammar, and suggest that the Biblical origin of the allusion is important, from a grammatical point of view, only for comparative study.
For the morphemes of Hebrew at one (possible) stage in the development of the language, see HARRIS, Journal of the American Oriental Society, vol. 61 (1941), p. 152-164.

5. — Clause builders form clauses (12). These clauses form larger structures. Some of these could be described as 'complex clauses'; groups of clauses bound to each other by certain particles (13). Other structures formed by clauses could be called 'bound structures', as they are bound together by chains of pronouns, all of which refer back to the same antecedent.
6. — In this view of the structure of Hebrew, all members of a lower level of structure are considered as being used in the one above it. Thus all morphemes form part of, or act as, words. All words form part of, or act as, clause-builders. All clause-builders are equally considered to form part of clauses, or to act as clauses themselves.
7. — Some particles fit into this scheme in a different way from other words. The term 'particle' refers to the third great division of traditional Semitic Grammar, containing all words which are not nouns (and pronouns), or verbs (and infinitives). Only a small number of these are members of the clause-builder class 'particle'. The term 'particle' has been used for this clause-builder class, despite the possibility of confusion, to avoid putting forward new terminology before a new classification of the Hebrew particles is firmly established. However a new classification must be made. The traditional terminology, borrowed from the European languages, is altogether too vague (14). The following is a tentative classification of the particles used in Qumrani prose.
1. Particles used at ‘word’ level of structure.
a) The article.
b) Prepositions (probably including 'T/'WT-) (15).
The 'clause-builder' level may seem to cover so wide an area as to be confusing. A single noun may function as an exponent of N, but so can a noun modified by several pN and pI elements. However the division of this level into further syntactic levels would be unlikely to add enough in clarity to compensate for its undoubted additions in complexity. For a description of their use in a group of clauses, see "Order". See below, § 7, section 3b. The following words are among those listed as 'adverbs' in KUHN's Kon-kordanz zu den Qumrantexter (Göttingen, 1960): 'Z, 'HR, 'MN, GM, LW', R'ŠWĦ, ŠM'WL. There is surely no criterion of structure or usage which obliges the analyst to put these particular words in one class. For instance if ŠM'WL is an adverb, why is not YMYN, which is used with ŠM'WL in all cases where it is not obviously a 'substantive'? Again BLTY is called a conjunction, despite the fact that, in all cases listed, it follows the preposition L- and negates an infinitival element. No doubt the title has some basis in Biblical Hebrew, but this is another example of uncritical reliance on traditional terminology. See 'Order', § 15.
E.J. REVELL
c) Negatives; particles which stand immediately before the word they modify, and negate it.
2. Particles used at the 'clause-builder' level of structure. Members of the clause-builder class pt (16).
3. Particles used at the clause level of structure.
a) Particles which stand before, and modify, verbal clauses. For example 'HR, 'Z, TRM (17).
b) Particles which join two clauses to form a complex clause. For example 'M, KY('), PN, 'ŠR (18).
4. Particles used at all levels of structure.
a) Conjunctions; for example 'W, W-, and probably KY(') 'M (19).
b) 'Emphatics'; Particles which stand immediately before the structure they modify, and mark it out or emphasize it. For example 'K, 'P, GM, RQ (20).
There are no doubt some changes to be made in this scheme of classification, but the main outline should remain valid for Qumrani prose. Many of the particles are used only rarely in the material available, and, since there is not enough evidence to ensure their correct classification, they have not been added to the list unless they are referred to in this article.
8. — Thus, although they are not all used on the word level of structure, all particles find a place in this scheme. They do not, therefore, give any cause to doubt the statement that all members of a lower level are used in the level above. Thus all clause-builders form part of, or act as, clauses. Since clause-builders can—at least in theory—act as clauses, it follows that clauses cannot always be recognized by their structure. In some cases they can only be recognized by their use (21). In fact only the verbal clause is easy to define. The definition of 'clause' on which this study must proceed is, then, 'any structure composed of one or more clause-builders which is used on the same structural level as verbal clauses'. The Verbal Clause
9. — As already stated, the only type of clause easy to define is the verbal clause. The simplest form of verbal clause is a verb form. This can be expanded by the addition of an exponent of Ns showing concord with the pronominal element in the verb form, and/or by the addition of one or more exponents of any of the other clause builders as modifiers of the verb. The majority of such clauses which occur in 1 Q S have been described in "Order". For the reasons given in "Order" note 4, however, clauses containing imperative verb forms were not included in that study. Some dozen imperative forms occur in the material studied in this paper. The clauses in which they occur do not differ in structure from other verbal clauses. They are therefore treated here as ordinary verbal clauses (23).
10. — The composition of the clause-building elements is largely the same in the other prose manuscripts as in 1 Q S. One This is, of course, based on the assumption, warranted in the case of literary, though not, perhaps, of spoken language, that the texts, in their original state, were made up of complete clauses. However the scribe does seem to have broken off in the middle of a clause in one or two cases; for example 1 Q Sa I, 12. Titles to sections of the text, the names of the trumpets and banners in 1 Q M, and clauses broken by lacunae, present further problems in non-continuous text. In all these cases the decision of whether or no to treat the passage as a clause is subjective, depending on whether or no the present author considers the passage to show clear clausal structure. Titles are discussed below in § 40. The names of trumpets and banners are not treated as clauses unless they contain a verb. The other instances can all be taken as single clause builders, although many of them could equally well be taken as two part clauses. Since they are not used in a context, there is no possibility of certainty. (See below, § 24). For the same reason––that their recognition is largely dependent on context—–very few non-verbal clauses damaged by lacunae have been included in the study. Verbal clauses are included when one end of the clause is preserved, and contains the verbal element and at least one other element. Broken clauses are also included if they appear to contain elements of particular interest, but such cases are noted where they are discussed. All the imperative forms in 1 Q S occur in Biblical quotations, or in poetical passages, and so are not included here. It should be noted here that verbal structures which form part of multipartite or 'ŠR clauses are described in the sections on those clauses (§ 25-35). All clauses containing verbs are not, therefore, described in this section. The clause-builders used in the verbal sections of those clauses do not, however, differ in structure or use from those used in the verbal clauses described here.
E. J. REVELL

To these can be added the possibility that NḤLT (1 Q SIV, 24) begins a nominal clause which follows a bound (construct) noun form. Clauses following bound nouns also occur in 1 Q M I, 10; XVII, 6. Clauses follow a preposition 1 Q MIX, 2; XVII, 9 and 1 Q p Hab X, 12-13. These positions are normally taken by nouns. The clauses are, therefore, noun substitutes.
11. — The particles used in the material from 1 Q S studied here are ‘WD and TMYD, which follow immediately after the verb they modify, and KN and KKH which immediately precede it. In the other manuscripts, ŠM and ‘ḤWR follow the verb immediately, BKN, KN, and MHR precede it immediately, MŠM and M’Z both precede and follow the verb. For the use of the particles ŠM and M’Z in ‘ŠR clauses, see notes 61 and 63.
12. — The only item which does not occur in 1 Q S, but which appears in the other prose manuscripts, is the ‘infinitive absolute’. Two examples of this occur, in the form HLWK W’WR, in a clause the structure of which is ]V-pN-inf. abs. structure-pI, in 1 Q M I, 8. With so few examples it is impossible to place the infinitive absolute in the structural scheme (24).

Nominal Clauses

In the following analysis of their structure, the more common types of nominal clause will be treated first. Other types will be dealt with under separate headings.

20. — The two parts of clauses of this type are usually called 'subject' and 'predicate'. It is, however, possible to justify the use of these terms in less than 25% of the clauses. The use of such terms to denote grammatical units is only justifiable if it can be shown that the units are distinguished by some grammatical marker. Thus the 'predicate' of a verbal clause is distinguished by the fact that it contains the verb. Where no such grammatical marker exists, it is obvious that the grounds on which 'subject' is distinguished from 'predicate' cannot be grammatical. They cannot, therefore, be treated as grammatical units.
21. — As type 1 shows, it is not necessary that either part of a two part nominal clause be an exponent of N (46). Consequently, even where one part of the clause does consist of an exponent of N, as in clause types 2-6, it is not necessarily the subject (47). Consequently one must admit that in clause types 1 to 6, the grammatical structure of the clauses provides no means of distinguishing subject and predicate.
22. — In clause type 7, where both parts of the clause are exponents of N, there are two possible ways in which subject and predicate might be grammatically distinguished. The traditional view of such clauses would suggest that the part of the
This is the standard pattern for blessing and curse formulae using the passive participle (BRWK, 'RWR , z'WM) where the participle has modifiers. The participle, the headword of the first part of the clause, stands first, and is immediately followed by the second part of the clause. The modifiers of the participle follow this 2nd. part. See also 1 Q M XIII, 2.4.4.5. This suggests that in 1 Q S II, 11 BGLWLY LBW L'BWR should not modify 'RWR, and indeed any translation I have seen which takes the text in this way is unconvincing, even when aided by emendation. The reading proposed by GASTER, 'RWR HB' BGLWLY LBW L'BWR (see The Scriptures of the Dead Sea Sect, London, 1957, p. 104, note 15) provides a text which is not only intelligible, but also conforms to Qumrani syntactical practices. (For a similar case of the misplacing of a few letters, compare Azitawadd inscription B II, 16-17 with A III, 13-14.)
It could be maintained that a pN element is, in these cases a noun substitute (see "Order", note 13). However if this explanation is used here, it can also be applied to transform pN elements in other clauses into possible nominal subjects.
An admirable illustration of the same problem in Biblical Hebrew occurs in BROCKELMANN'S Hebräische Syntax, § 27.b, where, in discussing a clause of the type pN-N, he calls the pN element the 'real, or psychological, subject', although traditionally he regards the exponent of N as the 'grammatical subject'. He is, of course, led to this conclusion by the context in which the clause occurs. On the importance of context, see below.

clause marked as definite should be the subject, and the part showing concord should be the predicate. As regards the first possibility, type 7g shows that both parts of a clause can be marked as definite. It cannot, therefore, be claimed that wherever one part of the clause is marked as definite it must be the subject (48).
23. — As regards the second possibility, the showing of concord does seem to be a true mark of the predicate. This occurs most commonly, of course, where the headword of one part of the clause is a participle or adjective. The participle or adjective (in the predicate) shows concord with the headword of the other part of the clause (the subject), which is normally marked as definite. However pronouns can also show concord, and the zH HSrk type of clause is probably to be included among those the predicate of which is marked by the fact that it shows concord with the subject. In this type of clause, the form of the pronoun (here zH, masculine singular) is determined by the following noun (here srk, masculine singular). This noun is marked as definite. The structure is therefore the same as in the typical nominal clause with participle or adjective as predicate. zH is predicate, and HSrk subject. This analysis seems perfectly logical, yet BROCKELMANN considers zH to be the subject in this type of clause (49). If he is right, this is a case of 'subject' showing concord with 'predicate'. Concord would not then be valid as indicator of the predicate.
24. — If BROCKELMANN is correct, therefore, there is no grammatical indicator which can be used to distinguish subject and predicate. If he is wrong, concord serves as an indicator of the predicate in about 25% of the clauses. In most nominal clauses, then, there is no grammatical marker within the clause which distinguishes 'subject' from 'predicate'. The conclusion that the division of such clauses into 'subject' and 'predicate' is irrelevant is inevitable. The two part nominal clause is, then, a structure formed of two clause-builders the relationship between which is shown by the context in which they occur, and not by any syntactical marker within the clauses themselves. In the majority of cases of type 7g, the first part of the clause is formed by HW'(H) , HY'(H), HMH or HNH. It can be shown to be likely that these pronouns are personal, and therefore definite, but this is not certain. There are three certain cases of the structure hN-hN: 'WRKYH KWL H'DH (1 Q M II, 9), 'NW 'M QWDŠKH (1 Q M XIV, 12) and HYWM MW'DW... (1 Q M XVII, 5). The restorations W['TH] 'L 'BWTYNW and W'NW 'M [GWR]L[KH] in 1 Q M XIII, 7 are highly probable, and would provide two further examples of this structure.
Hebräische Syntax, § 28.b.δ.
Multipartite Clauses
25. — A number of nominal clauses contain more than two parts. In three part clauses of this type, the second part is often a condensed repetition of the first, in many cases simply a pronoun. The second and third parts of a clause of this type could be taken as a two part clause. For instance,wkly MLḤMWTM / HMH / MWR'M I Q p Hab VI, 4-5.
26. — Some scholars in the past treated the pronoun in such clauses as a ‘copula’; a lexically negligible mark of the syntactic structure involved (50). However this explanation is not fitting. The term ‘copula’ carries with it the idea of ‘verb’, and the pronoun certainly has no connection at all with this function. Every verbal clause containing an exponent of Ns is, in fact, a tripartite clause of this type (51). In such clauses a nominal structure, Ns, is repeated by a pronoun, the pronoun in the verb form, which is followed by the third part of the clause, the verbal predicate. Compare kly MLḤMWTM / HMH / MWR'M with H'YŠ HNŠ'L / Y- / -DBR BTRW (I Q S VI, 11). The similarity of the two structures forbids the suggestion that the pronoun acts the part of copula in the one when it obviously does not in the other. Further cause the rejection of this theory can, if needed, be given by the fact that the second part of the clause need not be a pronoun, but can be a larger nominal structure. For example hdgl hmtqrb / kwlm / šB' m'rkwt (I Q M IX, 4). So also hwnm I Q S IX, 8.
27. — The second part of a clause of this type cannot, therefore, be considered a mere copula, but must, from a syntactical point of view, be equal in importance to the other two parts. Some scholars, realizing this, have interpreted such clauses as being basically bipartite. According to their analysis the first part of such a clause is a subject which is followed by a predicate which is itself a complete clause composed of subject and predicate (the second and third parts) (52). This view is somewhat complicated by the following considerations.
This explanation is still found in BROCKELMANN, Hebräische Syntax, § 30a.

In multipartite clauses, the N element which corresponds to the Ns element in verbal clauses (see the example below), always stands at the beginning of the clause and forms the first part of it.

28. — In the more complicated forms of this type of multi-p partite clause, where the last two parts form a verbal clause, the pronoun in these two parts which refers to, or repeats, the first part of the clause, need not function as the subject of this verbal clause. It may modify the verb of the predicate directly, as in wh'yš... yšlḥhw (1 Q S VII, 17). The pronoun may also merely form part of a structure modifying the verb, as in wkwl hn'šh bw yršh bndbh (1 Q S IX, 24). Although these clauses can be analyzed as composed of a subject followed by a predicate which is a complete clause, the relationship between the parts is obviously not the same as in the simpler type where the subject of the 'predicate clause' is the pronoun referring to the initial subject.
29. — The same type of structure is sometimes expanded to form a four part clause. As in the tripartite types, these may contain a verbal structure. For example kwl hb' ... / kwl 'yš mhmh... / y- /-šlḥhw (1 Q S VIII, 21-2). Examples which are purely nominal are also found. For instance pšrw / hqryh / hy' / yrwšlm (1 Q p Hab XII, 7). These clauses also could be explained as even more complicated convolutions of subject-predicate structure, but again this seems unnecessary. The conclusion reached after the study of the two part nominal clause was that the terms subject and predicate are irrelevant. The relationship between the parts of such a clause is indicated by the surrounding context, and not by any grammatical marker within the parts. This conclusion seems equally valid for three and four part clauses (53).
30. — The structure of multipartite clauses, seen in terms of clause-builders, is relatively simple. The first part of the clause is, in all the examples here studied, an exponent of N (54). In this study multipartite clauses are treated as single units, just as a verbal clause containing an exponent of Ns is a single unit, even though a complete verbal clause would still remain if the exponent of Ns were removed. The relationship between the parts of a multipartite clause is, of course, almost invariably marked by the noun or pronoun which repeats the first part in the second or third, but this can hardly be taken as an indicator of subject-predicate structure. It seems possible, but unlikely, that other elements can take this position. For example wl'wšr byd rmh lw' yšwb 'wd (1 Q S IX, 1) could perhaps be taken as a three part clause, although the explanation given in "Order"\(§ 22 and note 27) seems simpler. Similarly in two clauses opening with a pI element (1 Q M VII, 9-11; XVI, 11) and in one opening with a pN element (1 Q S IV, 24), this initial element is followed by a conjunction followed by an element of a different type. These have been taken as ordinary verbal clauses in this study. It is possible, however, that the use of a conjunction in a position of this sort is a mark of a multipartite clause. 31. — Clauses of multipartite structure are quite common. The material dealt with in this section is derived from only 32 three and four part clauses. This total does not, however, include verbal clauses containing an exponent of Ns, nor does it include ’ŠR clauses, many of which have tripartite structure.
’ŠR Clauses (57)
32. — Clauses introduced by ’ŠR can be divided into two types, according to their structure. In the first type, ’ŠR and the words following it form a two part clause (58). Since ’ŠR is a pronoun, id est a noun substitute, it can perform, in its clause, any function permissible to a noun. Clauses of this sort do not differ in structure from the two part clauses already described, except for the fact that, whatever its function in the clause, ’ŠR is always the first word.

The tenth one occurs in 1 Q S VI, 11-13, where the second part begins w’MD. The final example occurs in 1 Q M VII, 11-12, where the second part begins w’L HMQDŠ. As regards the use of the clause-builders of particular interest in these clauses: Ns and N appear together in only one case (1 Q S VI, 13-14). Here the exponent of N is a pronoun bound to the verb, and so stands between the exponent of Ns and the verbal element. There is one case of a pI element following the verb it modifies (1 Q Sa II, 4-8). The preposition is L-. No particles occur in these clauses. The ’ŠR discussed here is the Hebrew ‘relative’ pronoun. One of its characteristics is that it always stands as the first word in a clause. Verbal clauses containing exponents of Ns are also included in this group.

34. — The members of the second group of 'ŠR clauses are tripartite. Three part 'ŠR clauses are identical in structure to the three part clauses already described. They may either be purely nominal, or they may contain a verbal structure. In all cases the first part of the clause is a nominal element formed by the pronoun 'ŠR. In five cases the second and third parts of the clause form a nominal structure (62). In 34 cases the second and third parts form a verbal structure. In 33 of these, the element following the initial 'ŠR, the first part of the clause, is V. In the remaining example, an exponent of Ns stands between the 'ŠR and the V element. In five cases these verbal structures contain exponents of both Ns and N. In all cases both follow V. In two cases the exponent of Ns stands between the verbal element and the exponent of N. In the other three cases, the exponent of N is a pronoun bound to the verb form, and so stands between the verbal element and the exponent of Ns. The other elements in these verbal structures follow the order normal in verbal clauses (63).

36. — Once all the clause types described above have been isolated, the analyst is left with a relatively small number of structures which, in isolation, would not be recognized as clauses. These can be divided into two groups; ‘bound clauses’, which depend on the preceding context for the clarification of their structure, and one part clauses, which consist of a single ‘clause-builder’ used at clause level.
Bound Clauses

38. — A similar type of structure is found in nominal clauses. However here the term 'bound' is not so fitting, as a conjunction is often used to indicate the attachment of the 'bound clause' to the preceding clause. The structure is formed merely by the addition to a two part clause of a third clause-builder, of the same type as one of the original two, and usually joined to it by a conjunction. This third clause-builder forms the 'bound clause'. For example
hw'h qwrh bspr 'w mbrk (1 Q S VII, 1) N-N-cN,
ltwhw wlbhw tšwqtm (1 Q M XVII, 4) pN-cpN-N .
In some cases a conjunction is not used to join the bound clause to the preceding clause. For example:
hy'h ḥwmt hbḥn pnt yqr (1 Q S VIII, 7) N-N-N.
The above examples show only one clause bound to the initial two part clause, but there is no restriction on number (68). These clauses are listed as 'bound clauses' because of their similarity to the verbal 'bound clause'. They are, in fact, one part clauses (clauses made up of a single clause-builder), and could equally well have been listed in the next section.
One Part Clauses
39. — The remaining material in these texts falls into the category of one part clauses. These are single clause-builders in an unbroken context, which cannot be said to form part of other clauses. They are, therefore, used on the same syntactical level as clauses, and must be classed as clauses themselves. There are so few of these that it is possible to list them all.

'YN and YŠ Clauses
44. — One group of clauses, often set aside as a separate type, has not yet been treated. These are clauses containing 'YN and YŠ. They are set aside as a separate type on the grounds that these two particles have some verbal characteristics, and deserve the name 'predicate particles'. The most significant basis for this claim is probably the fact that they take 'verbal suffixes'. Id est personal pronouns, when bound to these particles assume a form used with the 'imperfect' form of the verb. However other particles, for which no verbal characteristics are claimed, take the same forms of bound pronoun (76). As far as syntax goes, the clauses in which 'YN and YŠ are used do not differ from other nominal clauses.
45. — 'YN should probably be classed as a negative (77). It is characteristic of the negatives in Qumrani Hebrew that they stand immediately before the word or structure that they modify, and do not bring about any change in the regular order of the clause building elements (78).
